screens.title: Understanding Requirements and Design Principles
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll build a reliable habit: define what the software must do, and then design how it will do it. Clear requirements are the foundation that prevents wasted work, rework, and mismatched expectations. You'll learn how to tell functional requirements — concrete actions the system must perform — from non-functional requirements, which are measurable quality targets like response time, scalability, and security. We'll also cover practical techniques for gathering requirements, from interviews to user stories, so your specifications are clear and testable. Then we'll move to software design: translating requirements into components, interfaces, and choices about architecture. Key principles — modularity, cohesion, and coupling — will help you split systems into manageable pieces, keep related behavior together, and minimize harmful dependencies. Throughout you'll see short examples for an online bookstore so you can practice writing both user stories and measurable NFRs. By the end you will understand how good requirements and disciplined design work together to make software easier to build, test, and evolve. Think about a feature you depend on daily: how would a vague requirement for it cause problems? That question will help you spot gaps as we proceed.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives will guide your work in this chapter so you graduate with skills you can use immediately. First, you will be able to distinguish functional from non-functional requirements, including writing clear examples that are measurable. That matters because teams need unambiguous acceptance criteria to avoid rework. Second, you will learn several effective techniques for gathering requirements — interviews, observation, surveys, and prototyping — and know when to use each so stakeholders’ needs are captured reliably. Each objective includes a concrete practice: write a user story or draft an NFR that is testable. Third, you will explain why software design exists in the lifecycle and how design decisions bridge requirements and implementation. This helps you choose architecture patterns deliberately rather than by accident. Fourth, you will identify and apply modularity, cohesion, and coupling so you can make small, safe changes in future iterations. For each objective you will see examples from an online bookstore so you can practice in a familiar context. These objectives are practical: they focus on producing testable artifacts and design choices you can validate with your team. As you work through the lesson, ask yourself which objective you want to practice first and why.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice and Assessment
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives connect to hands-on practice so you can show competency, not just recall facts. You'll write three functional requirements as user stories for an online bookstore, and three measurable non-functional requirements covering performance, security, and usability. This focused practice forces you to convert vague terms like "fast" into measurable targets such as load time under a specified percentile. You will also practice selecting gathering techniques: for a new checkout experience you might prototype a checkout flow, interview support staff for common issues, and run a short survey to prioritize features. Finally, you'll evaluate design using three principles: split the system into modules, ensure each module is responsible for a single purpose, and reduce unnecessary dependencies between modules. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you can self-assess or be assessed by a peer. These practical tasks are designed to be small, testable, and relevant to real teams. As you complete them, reflect on which technique revealed the clearest requirement and why that mattered for the design choices that followed.

screens.title: Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements
screens.narratorSegment: Start by defining the distinction clearly. Functional requirements specify observable behavior — actions users or other systems can request and that can be verified with tests. Examples include logging in, adding items to a cart, or generating reports. Non-functional requirements describe quality attributes: performance, scalability, availability, security, and usability. They don't list features; they set measurable expectations for those features. A common pitfall is writing vague NFRs like "the system should be fast." Instead, make them measurable: for example, "The dashboard must load within two seconds for 95% of requests." That small change makes the requirement testable and actionable for architects and operations. Consider an online bookstore: a functional requirement could be a user story that lets customers search by ISBN and add books to a shopping cart. A matching NFR might require the search results page to appear within 1.5 seconds under typical load. Notice how the NFR shapes infrastructure and design — caching, indexing, or autoscaling become relevant. A misconception to avoid is treating NFRs as optional extras; they often determine architecture and deployment patterns. As a takeaway, practice turning qualitative words into measurable targets. Which vague term in your last project could be rewritten as a clear, testable NFR?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Functional = actions the system performs; Non-functional = measurable quality attributes that guide design and operations.

content.html:
Definition
Functional vs Non-Functional
Clear definitions reduce ambiguity and make requirements testable.
Functional Requirements
Describe what the system must do. Example: "As a customer, I want to add items to a cart so I can buy multiple books."
Non-Functional Requirements
Describe how the system performs. Example: "Search results must load within 1.5 seconds for 90% of queries."
Common Mistake
Writing vague NFRs like "fast" or "secure" without measurable criteria. Fix by adding numbers, percentiles, or levels.
Concrete Example — Online Bookstore
Functional (User Story)
As a customer, I want to search for books by title or ISBN so that I can find desired items quickly.
Non-Functional (Measurable)
Performance: Search results must return within 1.5 seconds for 90% of queries during normal operation.
Key Takeaway

Always convert qualitative statements into measurable, testable criteria so design and operations can meet them.

screens.title: Functional Examples: Writing User Stories
screens.narratorSegment: User stories are a compact, human-centered way to capture functional requirements. The typical format — "As a [user], I want [action] so that [benefit]" — keeps the focus on value and rationale. Start with the user role: customer, admin, or guest. Next, specify the action in simple terms, then the reason that explains why it matters. For example, "As a customer, I want to search by ISBN so I can quickly locate a specific edition." That single line can be expanded into acceptance criteria like expected filters, edge cases, and success conditions. A common misconception is to confuse user stories with design: stories describe intent, not implementation. Avoid embedding implementation details like "use elasticsearch" in the story itself; reserve that for design tasks linked to the story. When writing multiple stories, keep them small and independent so teams can complete them in a single sprint. In practice, pair each user story with related NFRs — for search, pair a story with the measurable search latency requirement. Your exercise is to write three user stories for the online bookstore that are concise, independent, and include at least one acceptance criterion each. Which story will be easiest to verify with a test script?

keyIdea.title: User Stories
keyIdea.text: User stories express intent and value; acceptance criteria make them testable without prescribing implementation.

content.html:
Process
Write effective user stories
Keep stories focused on users, actions, and benefits. Pair with acceptance criteria.
Format
As a [user], I want [action] so that [benefit].
Acceptance Criteria
  • Describe testable outcomes and edge cases.
  • Keep criteria numeric or boolean where possible.
Misconception
Do not include implementation detail in the story. Implementation belongs to design tasks linked to the story.
Examples & Practice
As a customer, I want to search for books by title or ISBN so that I can find a specific edition.
Acceptance criteria:
- Results include exact ISBN matches and fuzzy title matches.
- Search returns within 1.5 seconds for 90% of queries.
As a customer, I want to add books to a shopping cart so that I can purchase multiple items.
Acceptance criteria:
- Cart persists for signed-in users across sessions.
- Adding an unavailable item returns a clear error.
Try This

Draft three user stories for checkout, search, and wish list, each with at least one clear acceptance criterion.

screens.title: Non-Functional Requirements: Measurable Quality Targets
screens.narratorSegment: Non-functional requirements specify quality attributes that inform architecture, deployment, and operational practices. Examples include performance goals, concurrency support, reliability, availability, and data security. These are not optional labels; they often dictate choices such as caching strategies, database sharding, or encryption libraries. For instance, specifying that the system must support 10,000 concurrent users without degradation means you must consider autoscaling, connection pooling, and load testing early. A frequent mistake is treating NFRs as afterthoughts — only addressed when problems emerge. Instead, capture them with measurable targets: response times with percentiles, concurrency limits, uptime percentages, and explicit encryption requirements. Security NFRs can state that all sensitive data must be encrypted at rest and in transit, which then shapes storage choices and TLS configurations. Usability NFRs can define acceptable error rates or task completion times for typical flows. When you write NFRs, include the measurement method and the context, for example load profile or peak hours. A useful exercise is to take a functional story and attach at least one NFR that would realistically change design. That pairing is essential: functionality without quality constraints leaves architects guessing.

keyIdea.title: NFRs Matter
keyIdea.text: Non-functional requirements are measurable constraints that shape architecture, deployment, and testing strategies; capture them early and specify how to measure them.

content.html:
Definition
Non-Functional Requirements
Quality attributes expressed as measurable targets that directly influence design and operations.
Performance
E.g., page load time < 2 seconds for 95% of requests during peak hours.
Scalability & Availability
E.g., system must support 10,000 concurrent users and be available 99.99% monthly.
Security
E.g., all user data encrypted at rest and in transit; role-based access controls enforced.
Example & Measurement
Scenario
If search must support high concurrency, you might add caching, index tuning, and horizontal scaling. The NFR specifies the target so you can validate design choices with load tests.
Exercise

Attach at least one measurable NFR to each of your three user stories and decide how you would test it.

Misconception
NFRs are not a checklist item; they often determine architecture and operational strategy and should be prioritized early.

screens.title: Gathering Requirements: Techniques and Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Capturing the right requirements requires selecting effective techniques for the context. Interviews are ideal for deep stakeholder knowledge — talk to product owners, support staff, and power users to uncover hidden needs. Surveys reach a broader audience quickly but tend to produce shallower answers; use them when you need prioritization data from many users. Observation reveals actual user behavior and uncovers workflow gaps that users may not articulate. Prototyping provides concrete artifacts for early feedback; a simple mock-up can expose misunderstandings before code is written. In Agile contexts, user stories and incremental prototypes work well together — write a story, validate it with a prototype, iterate the acceptance criteria. Each technique has trade-offs: interviews are time-consuming but rich, surveys scale but are less contextual, observation requires access to real workflows, and prototyping takes design time. A practical sequence is to start with interviews to define hypotheses, use surveys to quantify priorities, observe critical tasks to validate assumptions, and prototype high-risk flows. A common error is relying on a single method; mixing techniques reduces blind spots. After you gather requirements, document them clearly and link them to acceptance criteria so designers and testers can act without ambiguity. Which technique would you choose first for a checkout redesign, and why?

keyIdea.title: Gathering Techniques
keyIdea.text: Choose interviews for depth, surveys for scale, observation for real behavior, and prototypes for fast validation; combine methods to reduce risk.

content.html:
Process Flow
Choose and sequence requirement-gathering techniques
Practical workflow to discover accurate, testable requirements.
Interviews
Deep insights from stakeholders; uncover goals and constraints.
Surveys
Quantify preferences and prioritize features across many users.
Observation
See real workflows and pain points users may not articulate.
Prototyping
Validate ideas quickly with mock-ups and early user feedback.
Example Sequence
Interview product owner → run a short survey → observe checkout flow → prototype the top change.
Trade-offs
Interviews are rich but slow; surveys are fast but shallow; combine them to balance speed and depth.
Tip
Document decisions and link each requirement to its source and acceptance criteria for traceability.
Key Takeaway

Use a mix of techniques to capture clear, testable requirements and to reduce blind spots that lead to rework.

screens.title: User Story and NFR Templates
screens.narratorSegment: Templates reduce ambiguity and help a team capture the same level of detail consistently. Use the user story template for functional requirements and a short NFR template that specifies metric, threshold, and measurement method. For example, the user story template is 'As a [user], I want [action] so that [benefit].' Attach acceptance criteria with clear success conditions. An NFR template can be 'Quality attribute: [type]. Target: [metric and threshold]. Measurement: [method and context].' For instance: 'Performance. Target: 95th percentile page load time under 2 seconds during peak hours. Measurement: synthetic load tests with 1 minute sustained traffic simulating peak concurrency.' Always add context like peak traffic profile or expected data sizes. A common mistake is omitting the measurement method, which leaves testers guessing how to validate the NFR. When you practice, write both templates and supply an example for each of the three functional stories you created earlier. This exercise teaches you to think like both a product owner and an engineer — you describe value and provide the facts engineers need to implement and test it. Which of your stories benefited most from an attached NFR?

keyIdea.title: Templates
keyIdea.text: User story and NFR templates make requirements consistent and testable by specifying role, action, benefit, metric, threshold, and measurement.

content.html:
Code / Template
User Story & NFR Templates
Use these templates to standardize how teams record requirements and tests.
// User story template
As a [user role], I want [action] so that [benefit].

// Acceptance criteria (examples)
- Condition A is met.
- Condition B is met.

// NFR template
Quality attribute: [type]
Target: [metric and threshold]
Measurement: [method and context]
Concrete Example Attached
User story
As a customer, I want to filter search results by price and rating so that I can find books within my budget.
Attached NFR
Performance. Target: median filter response < 1 second under normal load. Measurement: automated UI tests with sample catalog of 50,000 items.
Key Takeaway

Always attach measurement and test method to each NFR so validation is straightforward.

screens.title: From Requirements to Design
screens.narratorSegment: Design is the bridge between what a system should do and how engineers will build it. When translating requirements into architecture, trace each requirement to design choices: which services, databases, or interfaces will satisfy it? High-impact NFRs guide those choices. For example, a requirement for very low latency search suggests different storage, indexing, and caching strategies than a system optimized for batch reporting. Begin with a high-level architecture that maps features to modules or services. Decide whether to use a microservices approach when teams need independent deployment and scaling, or a monolith when cross-cutting features and simplicity matter. Beware of deciding architecture based on preferences rather than requirements. The design process includes identifying components, defining interfaces, and selecting data flow patterns. Use simple component boxes and documented interfaces so teams can work in parallel. A common misconception is that architecture eliminates the need for good requirements — in fact, architecture without requirements is guessing. As a practical step, take one of your user stories and sketch a minimal set of components that would implement it, noting which NFRs influence each component. That mapping reveals trade-offs and helps prioritize work.

keyIdea.title: Design Purpose
keyIdea.text: Design maps requirements to components and interfaces; non-functional targets often determine architecture and operational constraints.

content.html:
Architecture
Translating Requirements to Components
Link each requirement to a component choice and interface so design decisions are traceable.
Traceability
Document which component satisfies each functional requirement and which components must meet each NFR.
Architecture Choice
Choose microservices for independent scaling and deployment, or a monolith for simplicity when appropriate, guided by requirements, not fashion.
Interface Design
Define clear APIs between components to reduce coupling and allow independent evolution.
Component Sketch — Search Feature
Search Service
Indexes queries and serves results; influenced by performance NFRs.
Catalog Database
Stores product data; consistency and scale needs affect schema and replication strategy.
Cache Layer
Used to meet low-latency NFRs and reduce load on index queries.
Key Takeaway

Map each requirement to components and interfaces; non-functional constraints often dictate infrastructure and patterns.

screens.title: Modularity: Breaking Systems into Components
screens.narratorSegment: Modularity is the practice of dividing a system into smaller, independent components that each have a clear responsibility. High modularity enables parallel development, easier testing, and incremental replacement. For example, an e-commerce system can separate authentication, product catalog, shopping cart, and payment processing. Each module encapsulates its data and logic so teams can work on one area without affecting others. A useful rule is the single responsibility idea: a module should do one thing well. When designing modules, choose clear interfaces and avoid sharing internal details. A common misconception is that more modules are always better; too much fragmentation increases operational complexity and overhead. Balance module boundaries with the team's ability to manage them. Measure cohesion within a module — high cohesion means the module's parts are strongly focused on the same purpose. Also design to limit coupling: modules should interact through minimal, well-defined interfaces. As an exercise, take one feature and propose a modular split, then identify which NFRs govern each module's behavior. That exercise makes trade-offs visible and helps you choose sensible boundaries. Modularity: Breaking Systems into Components means split systems into independent components with clear responsibilities to enable parallel work, testing, and replacement.. In practical terms, design systems as smaller, interchangeable parts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Modularity
keyIdea.text: Split systems into independent components with clear responsibilities to enable parallel work, testing, and replacement.

content.html:
Hierarchy
Modularity and Component Boundaries
Define modules around single responsibilities and well-defined interfaces.
Benefits
Parallel work, easier testing, independent deployment, and simpler reasoning about code.
Trade-off
Too many tiny modules add coordination and operational overhead; find a practical balance.
Example — Online Bookstore Modules
Authentication Module
Handles sign-in, tokens, and user sessions. Cohesion is high when it only manages authentication tasks.
Shopping Cart Module
Manages items, totals, and persistence across sessions. Keep data encapsulated to avoid tight coupling with order processing.
Payment Processing Module
Integrates with payment providers; isolate provider-specific logic behind interfaces to allow change.
Key Takeaway

Define module boundaries by responsibility, document interfaces, and balance granularity with operational cost.

screens.title: Cohesion: Keep Related Work Together
screens.narratorSegment: Cohesion measures how closely related the responsibilities inside a module are. High cohesion means that the module’s pieces all contribute to a single, well-defined purpose. This clarity reduces cognitive load, makes tests simpler, and localizes change when requirements evolve. For example, a module dedicated solely to payment processing should include payment validation, provider integration, and transaction logging for payments, not unrelated features like email campaigns. Low cohesion — when a module handles multiple unrelated responsibilities — leads to confusing code, mixed concerns, and fragile changes. Often low cohesion originates from convenience or accidental grouping of features. To evaluate cohesion, ask whether every function in the module would still belong there if the rest were removed. If the answer is no, consider splitting the module. Cohesion is improved by clear naming, focused interfaces, and tests that validate the module’s single responsibility. A misconception is that cohesion only affects code readability — it also impacts deployment, testing scope, and fault isolation. As practice, inspect a module in a recent project and list responsibilities; then propose a split that increases cohesion and explain how that reduces risk.

keyIdea.title: Cohesion
keyIdea.text: High cohesion groups related responsibilities so modules are focused, testable, and easier to change without side effects.

content.html:
Definition
Cohesion
High cohesion keeps related behavior together and limits unrelated responsibilities inside a module.
High Cohesion
All functions in the module serve a single purpose, making testing and reasoning straightforward.
Low Cohesion
A module handles unrelated tasks, causing maintenance headaches and hidden coupling.
Example & Exercise
Module A (low cohesion)
Handles authentication, profile updates, and sending notification emails — responsibilities that should be split.
Module B (high cohesion)
Handles only payment processing tasks and related validations.
Try This

Choose a module from a project, list its responsibilities, and propose a refactor to increase cohesion. Explain expected benefits.

screens.title: Coupling: Minimize Interdependence
screens.narratorSegment: Coupling measures how much one module depends on the internal details of another. Low coupling is desirable because it allows modules to change independently. Achieve low coupling by defining clear interfaces, using contracts like APIs, and avoiding shared mutable state. For example, if the shopping cart module depends only on a well-defined order interface, changes in payment processing are less likely to cascade. Tight coupling occurs when modules call each other's internals or share storage schemas directly, which forces coordinated changes and increases the risk of bugs. In distributed systems, coupling also affects deployment and scaling: tightly coupled services may need to be deployed together, undermining the benefits of microservices. A common misconception is that decoupling always requires complex patterns; often simple A P I boundaries and small data contracts are sufficient. When designing for low coupling, consider fault boundaries and graceful degradation: design modules so failures in one do not bring down the whole system. As a practical check, list module dependencies and ask whether each dependency could be replaced without altering the dependent module's internal code. If not, the boundary needs improvement.

keyIdea.title: Coupling
keyIdea.text: Low coupling reduces risk by keeping module dependencies minimal and based on stable interfaces, enabling independent evolution and deployment.

content.html:
Comparison
Tight vs Loose Coupling
Aim for well-defined interfaces to reduce the blast radius of changes.
Tight Coupling
Modules depend on each other's internals or share schema; changes require coordinated updates and risk regression.
Loose Coupling
Interactions occur via stable interfaces or APIs; modules can evolve and be deployed independently.
Example & Checklist
Example
If the cart relies only on an order API, a payment provider change does not require cart changes. That is loose coupling.
Coupling Checklist
  • Does the module expose a minimal API?
  • Is shared state avoided?
  • Can the dependency be swapped with a mock in tests?
Key Takeaway

Minimize knowledge about other modules’ internals and design stable contracts to reduce the cost and risk of change.

screens.title: Common Design Mistakes and Practical Remedies
screens.narratorSegment: Teams commonly fall into a few recurring traps when moving from requirements to design. Tight coupling is one — modules become interdependent and fragile, making routine updates risky. The remedy is to refactor toward clear A P I boundaries, add abstractions only where they add value, and introduce tests that allow safe changes. Low cohesion appears when modules accumulate unrelated responsibilities. The fix is to split the module along responsibility lines, and move shared utilities into a small, well-documented utility module. Over-engineering is another hazard: designing for hypothetical future features that may never arrive. Prefer YAGNI — you aren't going to need it — and focus on meeting current, prioritized requirements plus reasonable extensibility. Another practical tip is to codify traceability: link each design decision to the requirement it serves, so you can revisit choices when requirements change. Finally, treat NFRs as first-class citizens: include them in backlog refinement and design reviews. A final reflective question for you: which of these mistakes is most likely in your team, and what small step can you take this week to prevent it?

keyIdea.title: Remedies
keyIdea.text: Refactor to clear boundaries, split responsibilities, avoid premature optimization, and make NFRs part of design conversations.

content.html:
Best Practices
Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
Concrete remedies you can apply in planning and design reviews.
Tight Coupling
Refactor using API boundaries, introduce adapter patterns, and write integration tests to validate contracts.
Low Cohesion
Split responsibilities into focused modules and move cross-cutting concerns to shared services as needed.
Over-Engineering
Avoid designing for unlikely futures; prioritize current NFRs and allow controlled extension points.
Traceability
Link requirements to design decisions so the team can revisit choices when requirements change.
NFRs in Planning
Include NFRs during backlog grooming and design reviews; treat them as acceptance criteria for architecture work.
Action

This week, pick one module and run a five-minute cohesion check: list responsibilities and decide what can be split or clarified.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's quickly summarize three core concepts you should remember. First, functional requirements state what the system must do and are usually expressed as user stories with acceptance criteria. Second, non-functional requirements describe how the system should perform — they must be measurable and include the method of measurement because they drive architecture and operations. Third, software design principles like modularity, cohesion, and coupling help you structure systems so they are maintainable and resilient; aim for high cohesion within modules and low coupling between them. These three ideas form a chain: clear requirements enable targeted design, and disciplined design makes the system easier to change and test. Keep practicing by turning vague requirements into measurable statements and mapping each requirement to design choices. Which one of these ideas will you apply first in your next project?

keyIdea.text: Functional vs NFRs, measurable quality targets, and modular design principles are the foundation of robust software.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build a reliable habit: define what the software must do, and then design how it will do it. Clear requirements are the foundation that prevents wasted work, rework, and mismatched expectations. You'll learn how to tell functional requirements — concrete actions the system must perform — from non-functional requirements, which are measurable quality targets like response time, scalability, and security. We'll also cover practical techniques for gathering requirements, from interviews to user stories, so your specifications are clear and testable. Then we'll move to software design: translating requirements into components, interfaces, and choices about architecture. Key principles — modularity, cohesion, and coupling — will help you split systems into manageable pieces, keep related behavior together, and minimize harmful dependencies. Throughout you'll see short examples for an online bookstore so you can practice writing both user stories and measurable NFRs. By the end you will understand how good requirements and disciplined design work together to make software easier to build, test, and evolve. Think about a feature you depend on daily: how would a vague requirement for it cause problems? That question will help you spot gaps as we proceed.

These objectives will guide your work in this chapter so you graduate with skills you can use immediately. First, you will be able to distinguish functional from non-functional requirements, including writing clear examples that are measurable. That matters because teams need unambiguous acceptance criteria to avoid rework. Second, you will learn several effective techniques for gathering requirements — interviews, observation, surveys, and prototyping — and know when to use each so stakeholders’ needs are captured reliably. Each objective includes a concrete practice: write a user story or draft an NFR that is testable. Third, you will explain why software design exists in the lifecycle and how design decisions bridge requirements and implementation. This helps you choose architecture patterns deliberately rather than by accident. Fourth, you will identify and apply modularity, cohesion, and coupling so you can make small, safe changes in future iterations. For each objective you will see examples from an online bookstore so you can practice in a familiar context. These objectives are practical: they focus on producing testable artifacts and design choices you can validate with your team. As you work through the lesson, ask yourself which objective you want to practice first and why.

These objectives connect to hands-on practice so you can show competency, not just recall facts. You'll write three functional requirements as user stories for an online bookstore, and three measurable non-functional requirements covering performance, security, and usability. This focused practice forces you to convert vague terms like "fast" into measurable targets such as load time under a specified percentile. You will also practice selecting gathering techniques: for a new checkout experience you might prototype a checkout flow, interview support staff for common issues, and run a short survey to prioritize features. Finally, you'll evaluate design using three principles: split the system into modules, ensure each module is responsible for a single purpose, and reduce unnecessary dependencies between modules. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you can self-assess or be assessed by a peer. These practical tasks are designed to be small, testable, and relevant to real teams. As you complete them, reflect on which technique revealed the clearest requirement and why that mattered for the design choices that followed.

Start by defining the distinction clearly. Functional requirements specify observable behavior — actions users or other systems can request and that can be verified with tests. Examples include logging in, adding items to a cart, or generating reports. Non-functional requirements describe quality attributes: performance, scalability, availability, security, and usability. They don't list features; they set measurable expectations for those features. A common pitfall is writing vague NFRs like "the system should be fast." Instead, make them measurable: for example, "The dashboard must load within two seconds for 95% of requests." That small change makes the requirement testable and actionable for architects and operations. Consider an online bookstore: a functional requirement could be a user story that lets customers search by ISBN and add books to a shopping cart. A matching NFR might require the search results page to appear within 1.5 seconds under typical load. Notice how the NFR shapes infrastructure and design — caching, indexing, or autoscaling become relevant. A misconception to avoid is treating NFRs as optional extras; they often determine architecture and deployment patterns. As a takeaway, practice turning qualitative words into measurable targets. Which vague term in your last project could be rewritten as a clear, testable NFR?

User stories are a compact, human-centered way to capture functional requirements. The typical format — "As a [user], I want [action] so that [benefit]" — keeps the focus on value and rationale. Start with the user role: customer, admin, or guest. Next, specify the action in simple terms, then the reason that explains why it matters. For example, "As a customer, I want to search by ISBN so I can quickly locate a specific edition." That single line can be expanded into acceptance criteria like expected filters, edge cases, and success conditions. A common misconception is to confuse user stories with design: stories describe intent, not implementation. Avoid embedding implementation details like "use elasticsearch" in the story itself; reserve that for design tasks linked to the story. When writing multiple stories, keep them small and independent so teams can complete them in a single sprint. In practice, pair each user story with related NFRs — for search, pair a story with the measurable search latency requirement. Your exercise is to write three user stories for the online bookstore that are concise, independent, and include at least one acceptance criterion each. Which story will be easiest to verify with a test script?

Non-functional requirements specify quality attributes that inform architecture, deployment, and operational practices. Examples include performance goals, concurrency support, reliability, availability, and data security. These are not optional labels; they often dictate choices such as caching strategies, database sharding, or encryption libraries. For instance, specifying that the system must support 10,000 concurrent users without degradation means you must consider autoscaling, connection pooling, and load testing early. A frequent mistake is treating NFRs as afterthoughts — only addressed when problems emerge. Instead, capture them with measurable targets: response times with percentiles, concurrency limits, uptime percentages, and explicit encryption requirements. Security NFRs can state that all sensitive data must be encrypted at rest and in transit, which then shapes storage choices and TLS configurations. Usability NFRs can define acceptable error rates or task completion times for typical flows. When you write NFRs, include the measurement method and the context, for example load profile or peak hours. A useful exercise is to take a functional story and attach at least one NFR that would realistically change design. That pairing is essential: functionality without quality constraints leaves architects guessing.

Capturing the right requirements requires selecting effective techniques for the context. Interviews are ideal for deep stakeholder knowledge — talk to product owners, support staff, and power users to uncover hidden needs. Surveys reach a broader audience quickly but tend to produce shallower answers; use them when you need prioritization data from many users. Observation reveals actual user behavior and uncovers workflow gaps that users may not articulate. Prototyping provides concrete artifacts for early feedback; a simple mock-up can expose misunderstandings before code is written. In Agile contexts, user stories and incremental prototypes work well together — write a story, validate it with a prototype, iterate the acceptance criteria. Each technique has trade-offs: interviews are time-consuming but rich, surveys scale but are less contextual, observation requires access to real workflows, and prototyping takes design time. A practical sequence is to start with interviews to define hypotheses, use surveys to quantify priorities, observe critical tasks to validate assumptions, and prototype high-risk flows. A common error is relying on a single method; mixing techniques reduces blind spots. After you gather requirements, document them clearly and link them to acceptance criteria so designers and testers can act without ambiguity. Which technique would you choose first for a checkout redesign, and why?

Templates reduce ambiguity and help a team capture the same level of detail consistently. Use the user story template for functional requirements and a short NFR template that specifies metric, threshold, and measurement method. For example, the user story template is 'As a [user], I want [action] so that [benefit].' Attach acceptance criteria with clear success conditions. An NFR template can be 'Quality attribute: [type]. Target: [metric and threshold]. Measurement: [method and context].' For instance: 'Performance. Target: 95th percentile page load time under 2 seconds during peak hours. Measurement: synthetic load tests with 1 minute sustained traffic simulating peak concurrency.' Always add context like peak traffic profile or expected data sizes. A common mistake is omitting the measurement method, which leaves testers guessing how to validate the NFR. When you practice, write both templates and supply an example for each of the three functional stories you created earlier. This exercise teaches you to think like both a product owner and an engineer — you describe value and provide the facts engineers need to implement and test it. Which of your stories benefited most from an attached NFR?

Design is the bridge between what a system should do and how engineers will build it. When translating requirements into architecture, trace each requirement to design choices: which services, databases, or interfaces will satisfy it? High-impact NFRs guide those choices. For example, a requirement for very low latency search suggests different storage, indexing, and caching strategies than a system optimized for batch reporting. Decide whether to use a microservices approach when teams need independent deployment and scaling, or a monolith when cross-cutting features and simplicity matter.
